video.title: Summer League Fact Or Fiction: Recapping The Eastern Conference

summary: Josh Lloyd goes through the Eastern Conference summer league teams in reverse alphabetical order and reviews the rookies, second year players and two-way players worth discussing. He liked AJ Dybantsa's free throw rate and defensive stats despite poor shooting. He felt proven right on Allen Graves, Labaron Philon Jr. and especially Meleek Thomas, who was the top fantasy player of summer league. He was impressed by Egor Demin, Jase Richardson, Noah Penda, Braden Burries and Chris Cenac, and he considers Jalen Slawson far too good for a two-way deal. He was very down on Dailyn Swain, Nate Ament, Ben Saraf, Danny Wolf and Drake Powell. He warns that Caleb Wilson's hot shooting start may be fool's gold and that he could go too high in drafts.

rules.text: Summer league shooting percentages do not mean much. Look for whether the skills that made the player good showed up.
rules.quote: shooting percentages in the summer league don't really mean anything. What we want to see is the things that made you good.

rules.text: Summer league percentages have some correlation for rookies, but not for second year players.
rules.quote: when we talk about those correlation numbers, that's on rookies, not on second year guys.

rules.text: Summer league rules such as 10 fouls and single free throw attempts can distort free throw numbers.
rules.quote: they tried out this new free throw situation where you only get one attempt. So, the percentages can be off.

rules.text: Judge summer league stats in context. On a team with no other talent, high usage and big scoring should be expected.

rules.text: A summer league team with many main roster players usually means the NBA team will be bad.
rules.quote: a summer league team that's filled with like nine rotation or sorry nine main roster players it probably means that team is going to be bad.

rules.text: Second year players should dominate summer league. Ordinary numbers from them are a disappointment.
